title: Code after return
summary: Learn why Java rejects a statement that must come after return, and how to trace which paths can reach each line.
objectives: Explain that `return` leaves the current method immediately.
Tell the difference between a compile-time unreachable statement and a line skipped at run time.
Trace a method to decide whether each line can run.
Fix code that puts a statement after an unconditional `return`.

blocks.text: A `return` statement leaves the current method immediately. A common mistake is to put a statement after a `return` that always runs first. That later statement can never run. Java detects this before the program runs and reports an unreachable statement.

bad.title: The print can never run

good.title: Return, then print in the caller

blocks.note: The first program does not compile, so it never runs. The compiler rejects the print because `return 7;` always leaves `getValue` first. In the fixed version, the caller prints after the method has returned.

blocks.text: Control flow means the order in which statements run. Java normally goes from one statement to the next. But `return` changes that order: it exits the current method. The compiler can see when every path to a line has already returned, so it reports that line as unreachable at compile time. This is not a run-time crash or a warning.

blocks.caption: A return ends this path through the method
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B{stop is true}
  B -- yes --> C[Return from method]
  B -- no --> D[Print continued]
  C --> E([End])
  D --> E

blocks.text: The diagram shows why a line after an `if` can still be reachable: when `stop` is false, the method skips the `return` and reaches the print. That differs from a `return` that runs unconditionally before the print.

blocks.title: Compile time and run time
blocks.text: Compile time is when Java checks and translates your code. Run time is when a compiled program runs. An unconditional `return` followed by another statement is rejected at compile time. A line that is skipped on one run-time path may still be reachable on another path, so it can compile.

sections.title: Trace it, one step at a time

blocks.text: Tracing means following the statements in order and noting what happens. Consider `if (stop) return;` followed by `System.out.println("continued");`. Trace one call with `stop` set to `true`.

blocks.caption: Tracing one call when stop is true

blocks.text: Now trace with `stop = false`. The `return` does not run, so the method reaches the print. Since at least one path can reach that line, it is not unreachable to the compiler.
First, compare an unconditional return with a conditional one. The first example above fails during compilation. This complete program shows a conditional return that can be skipped.
The first call returns before printing. The second call does not return at the `if`, so it prints `continued`. The `return` only exits `show`; it does not end the whole program.

blocks.title: How to fix an accidental unreachable line
items: Find the `return` that runs before the line you wanted.
Ask whether the method should return before doing that work.
If the work must happen first, move it before the `return`.
If the work belongs after the method returns, put it in the caller, as in the `ReturnFixed` example.

blocks.text: The mistake can be less obvious when the `return` is inside a branch. Ask whether every possible path to the later statement has already returned.

bad.title: Both branches return before the print

blocks.note: In the bad version, either branch exits the method, so the print cannot be reached and Java reports an unreachable statement. In the good version, the print happens before either branch returns.
The bad order leaves the method before the update. The update is unreachable and cannot change the returned value. Put the work before `return` when the returned value should include it.

blocks.title: Check the path, not just the next line
blocks.text: A line after `if (stop) return;` can run when `stop` is false. A line after an unconditional `return`, or after branches that all return, cannot run.

blocks.question: What happens when Java compiles this method?
options: It compiles, but skips the print at run time.
The compiler reports an unreachable statement.
blocks.explanation: `return 4;` always exits the method before the print. Java reports the print as unreachable at compile time, so the method does not compile.

blocks.question: Can the print run when `stop` is false?
options: Yes. The condition is false, so the method reaches the print.
No. Any `return` makes all later lines unreachable.
No. The compiler rejects every line after an `if`.
Yes, but only after the method has ended.
blocks.explanation: When `stop` is false, the body containing `return` is skipped. The method continues to the print, so that line is reachable.

blocks.question: What does `return;` do inside a `void` method?
options: It leaves the current method immediately.
It ends every method in the program.
It pauses the method and then continues.
blocks.explanation: A `return;` in a `void` method exits that method immediately. The print after it is unreachable, so Java reports an error at compile time.

items: A statement after an unconditional `return` cannot run, and Java reports it as unreachable at compile time.
A line after a conditional `return` can still be reachable if another path skips the return.
Trace each path in order. Check whether any path can reach the line.
Move needed work before the `return`, or put work that belongs after a method call in the caller.
